title: Is Email Feedback a Waste of Time?
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline responds to Tom Sherrington's argument that feedback delivered via email after a lesson observation is fundamentally flawed -- one-directional, uninformed by the teacher's context, and, in Sherrington's words, 'outright rude.' Cline largely agrees with Sherrington's underlying principles but pushes back on the practical conclusion, describing his school's two-tier coaching system: intensive instructional coaching for a small cohort, and termly 'drop-in' observations with written feedback for the rest of staff, given time and resource constraints. He argues via a cost-benefit lens that email feedback, while imperfect, is generating real behaviour change when it always leads with genuine positive feedback and frames critique as evidence-based questions rather than directives. He closes by thanking Sherrington for the ironically non-dialogic blog post that pushed his own thinking forward.
points: Cline summarises Sherrington's core objections to email feedback: it isn't dialogic, isn't co-constructed, ignores the receiving teacher's context and state, and can read as 'outright rude.'
He counters with a practical cost-benefit framing: given real school resource constraints, is the current system 'causing more harm than good?' -- and argues it is net positive even though imperfect.
His school's feedback practice always leads with genuine, specific positive feedback, and frames critique as an evidence-based question rather than a directive.
He acknowledges the irony that Sherrington's own blog post -- itself less direct and dialogic than an email -- was what actually changed his thinking.
quotes: Feedback is best when it is co-constructed between both parties, rather than simply transmitted by the observer.

Feedback sent via email doesn't really afford any of the above, and so is unlikely to be helpful. It probably won't lead to a teacher actually changing their practice. In fact, Tom describes this as outright rude.

So should we just ditch email feedback? I’m not sure. I think part of this comes down to playing the percentages game and considering a cost-benefit analysis – do I think this system is causing more harm than good?
It's not 'You did X, you should have done Y' rather it's 'I noticed X happened when you did Y. What might have happened if you'd tried Z instead?'
So thank you, Tom. This was useful feedback that I’m responding to. And, ironically, it was a blogpost that did this, something even less direct, personalised and co-constructed than an email!
